stories.headline: Australia's fuel crisis deepens: Albanese conducts SE Asia energy diplomacy, Geelong refinery fire, Hormuz summit, and Trump criticism
stories.summary: The Iran war-driven global oil shock dominated Australian politics this week. PM Albanese travelled to Brunei and Malaysia to secure fuel and fertiliser supplies, the Geelong Viva Energy refinery caught fire reducing petrol production by 40%, Albanese joined a ~50-nation virtual summit co-hosted by Macron and Starmer on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump publicly criticised Australia for not doing enough to assist. Albanese rejected Trump's claim that new requests had been made and denied the country would move to fuel rationing. The Strait briefly reopened before Iran closed it again.

stories.headline: Angus Taylor's 'values-based' immigration policy draws racist charge from Keating and internal Liberal concern
stories.summary: Opposition Leader Angus Taylor announced a hardline immigration policy pledging Trump-style social media vetting, deportation of migrants who fail 'Australian values' standards, and singling out Gazan arrivals as security risks. The policy drew a blistering attack from former PM Paul Keating labelling it 'cowardly and racist,' criticism from Liberal moderates who worry it will cost urban seats, and broad media debate. Taylor defended the policy as a values-first reset and unveiled it alongside former PM John Howard.

stories.headline: RBA signals further rate hikes as fuel shock risks stagflation; Deputy Governor Hauser warns of 'central banker's nightmare'
stories.summary: RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser gave multiple speeches warning that Australia entered the Iran oil shock 'already running hot,' that the central bank lacks 'high confidence' rates are at the right level, and that stagflation risks have emerged. Employment data for March came in broadly in line with forecasts (unemployment steady at 4.3%), reinforcing hawkish RBA policy expectations. Markets priced a ~65% chance of a further rate hike to 4.35% at the May meeting. Consumer sentiment collapsed.

stories.headline: Australia and Japan sign $7 billion warship contracts for 11 Mogami-class frigates
stories.summary: Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles and Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi signed contracts aboard the frigate JS Kumano in Melbourne on Saturday for the first three of 11 Mogami-class frigates, marking Japan's largest-ever defence export and deepening bilateral security ties. The first three vessels will be built in Japan with delivery expected from 2029, followed by a transition to onshore construction at Henderson shipyard in Western Australia.

stories.headline: Australia releases 2026 National Defence Strategy with $305–$425 billion decade-long spending commitment
stories.summary: The Albanese government released its 2026 National Defence Strategy and Integrated Investment Program, pledging to boost defence spending to approximately 3% of GDP by 2033. Defence Minister Marles framed it as addressing Australia's 'most complex and threatening strategic circumstances since World War II.' The plan drew criticism from private sector investors who were unenthusiastic about proposals for superannuation funds to supplement defence spending. A separate analysis flagged tension between funding AUKUS and conventional force modernisation simultaneously.

stories.headline: AUKUS submarine budget blows out to $96 billion; new ADF chief Mark Hammond travels to US for Iran and AUKUS briefings
stories.summary: Updated Defence Department figures revealed the AUKUS submarine program could cost up to $96 billion over the decade, a one-third blowout, while the total 30-year AUKUS cost was confirmed at $368 billion. Incoming Chief of the Defence Force Vice Admiral Mark Hammond travelled to the United States for briefings on the Iran war and the AUKUS nuclear submarine project. BAE Systems Australia launched a new supply chain qualification programme for Australian industry to support SSN-AUKUS construction.

stories.headline: Ben Roberts-Smith charged with five counts of war crime murder; vows to fight charges
stories.summary: Australia's most decorated living soldier, Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith, publicly denied all allegations after being charged with five counts of the war crime of murder relating to alleged killings of unarmed Afghan civilians during his SAS service. Roberts-Smith stated he would take the opportunity to clear his name. Australia has never previously held a war crimes trial for one of its own soldiers.

stories.headline: Federal polls show Labor ahead of Coalition; One Nation slides from historic highs
stories.summary: Multiple polling surveys released this week (Newspoll, Resolve Political Monitor, DemosAU, Morgan) showed Labor maintaining a lead on a two-party preferred basis, One Nation's primary vote dipping from historic peaks, and Angus Taylor's net approval declining. The polls were conducted during the week Albanese was abroad managing the energy crisis and Taylor launched his immigration policy. Labor's preferred PM lead remained at 46% vs Taylor's 37%.
